name: Manvi Mehrotra
description: Built HTMLHub so teammates can securely host and share the HTML prototypes they create with AI.
title: A secure home for AI-built prototypes.
challengeTitle: Sharing a prototype needs more than an HTML file.
challenge: Teams were using Claude, GPT and other AI tools to create interactive HTML dashboards, reports, prototypes and pitch decks. Creating the file was only the first step: the people who needed to review it still needed a reliable way to open it.

A localhost link worked only on the creator’s machine. Emailing an attachment moved the file around, while a screenshot lost the interactivity that made the prototype useful. Sharing the output in a Slack thread did not solve the hosting or access problem.

Manvi built HTMLHub as a central place to upload, host and share those outputs inside Cars24. The next challenge was helping that collection grow into team-owned workspaces, where people could find the right document, update it without changing its link, and discuss it in context.
solutions: Upload once, share a live link

HTMLHub turns an uploaded HTML file into a hosted page, so teammates can review the interactive output without running it on their own machine or needing engineering help. V1 supported sharing with specific teammates or the approved company domains, with access that could be revoked.
Put access controls around the work

The launch placed files behind Cloudflare Access for employee-only access. V2 added administrator controls for viewing versus downloading, alongside visibility into users, shares and permissions. That made access management part of the hosting workflow.
Give teams a lasting workspace

V2 introduced Spaces so the team, rather than only an individual, could own its collection of documents. HTML updates retained the same share link, letting people return to an updated dashboard or report without chasing a replacement URL.
Keep review beside the document

V2 brought comments, teammate mentions and resolved discussions into the HTML itself. CLI uploads and Markdown support extended the workflow to reports, RFCs and AI-generated outputs, while dark mode followed the user’s system preference.
outcomeTitle: From shared files to a team workspace.
outcomes: A platform people were using
In her 28 April 2026 update, Manvi reported 770+ users, 760+ documents and 850 share links since the V1 launch. The same update reported 461 new users and 507 uploads over the preceding 30 days.
A broader workflow in V2

The V2 release combined team-owned Spaces, stable links, access controls and in-document collaboration. These were reported product capabilities; external sharing, direct AI integrations and version history were listed as future V3 work.
productAlt: HTMLHub V2 Spaces interface with team workspaces and project collections
statsAsOf: Reported 28 April 2026, following the V1 launch.

name: Vishal Thakur
description: Built an AI support bot that reads Slack threads, suggests troubleshooting and routes unresolved issues to the right team.
title: Bringing IT support into the Slack conversation.
challengeTitle: The support request starts in a thread.
challenge: IT and product-support requests arrive as Slack threads containing error messages, URLs, screenshots and follow-up explanations. A useful first response needs that context and should leave room for the support team to answer first.

Vishal built an in-house support bot with Claude as a co-pilot. It monitors support channels, waits for a human response and, when needed, offers issue-specific troubleshooting before routing unresolved cases to the correct owner.

The design also needed clear limits. Access requests must reach the right team rather than trigger an automated access change, and a bot should not confirm an outage without evidence or recommend bypassing security controls.
solutions: Read the whole support thread

The bot considers the full thread, including error messages, shared URLs and usable screenshots. It also detects duplicate or recurring issues, preserves thread context and restores recently unanswered tickets after a restart.
Give the team the first response

The workflow allows a five-minute response window for IT or support engineers. If an engineer replies, the bot stays silent. Otherwise it posts safe, issue-specific troubleshooting rather than competing with a human response.
Route unresolved work to its owner

Unresolved cases are directed to the correct team or owner under defined SOPs. Access changes are routed to a support mailbox or team and are never performed by the bot. Optional network diagnosis can use read-only device-status data.
Roll out channel by channel

The August launch reported active monitoring in three support channels. A fourth channel remained in silent-study mode, learning from approved engineer resolutions without posting replies. Internal-platform integration was described as a later phase.
outcomeTitle: An AI support bot, launched in production.
outcomes: Production support inside Slack
Vishal reported the production launch on 28 August 2026. The bot covered connectivity, VPN, workplace-tool requests, access and mapping requests, SIM issues, and application or login errors.
A staged rollout with defined boundaries

The release separated active support channels from silent study and kept access changes with the responsible people. The next planned steps were API/authentication integration, user-context mapping and a controlled internal-platform pilot.

name: Ayush Gupta
description: Led an AI dealer-engagement pilot that uses conversation and inventory context to personalise outreach, then added a daily improvement loop.
title: Making dealer outreach respond to the conversation.
challengeTitle: Outreach needs the context behind it.
challenge: Dealer outreach was being scheduled largely through judgement and routine calls. The launch post described a gap in deciding the right time and frequency for each dealer using the information the business already held.

Ayush built a pilot that uses previous conversations, new inventory and Zendesk context to decide whom to call and prepare a personalised briefing for the voicebot. It connects Snowflake data to AutoLMS through Helios.

The next step was to improve the outreach agent using the calls themselves. A July update described a second agent that reviews call transcripts and outcomes, diagnoses problems, proposes changes and tests them before they go live.
solutions: Choose the dealer using context

The pilot scans previous conversations, new inventory and Zendesk information to identify eligible dealers. It prepares a short dealer-specific context for the voicebot to read before a call, rather than treating each outreach attempt as a fresh conversation.
Connect the calling workflow

The workflow pushes data from Snowflake to AutoLMS through Helios. The voicebot can use curated inventory, production tools and a retrieval-based knowledge base covering dealer SOPs, pricing data and tool specifications. Priyanshu Jha built and delivered the integration APIs.
Run outreach on a schedule

The July update reported three daily runs across two Helios jobs, with panel-editable rules. The workflow selects eligible dealers, writes personalised context and dispatches calls without a manual trigger for each run.
Test improvements before release

A daily improvement agent reads transcripts, call evaluations and downstream outcomes from Snowflake, then identifies a funnel leak and updates the voicebot. The reported release gate used 17 evaluation criteria and 17 automated tests, with backups, diffs and safety checks.
outcomeTitle: A production pilot with a daily improvement loop.
outcomes: A pilot followed by an improvement loop
The Gujarat and Pune pilot was reported live on 27 June 2026. By the 12 July update, the outreach workflow was running automatically and the daily improvement agent was reviewing and testing changes.
Early signals, with uncertainty kept visible

Ayush reported an early increase in bids per dealer in the called group, while explicitly saying the held-out control still had limited statistical significance. This was an early pilot signal, rather than a proven conversion uplift.
productAlt: Dealer engagement workflow shared with the June pilot: context selection, call briefing and dispatch

name: Ayush Upadhyay
description: Built an automated build–test–fix–validate loop for voice agents. His July update reported two follow-up campaigns deployed to production.
title: Building an agent that builds and tests voice agents.
challengeTitle: The work continues after the first build.
challenge: An ElevenLabs voice agent needs more than an initial prompt. Its workflow and tools must be configured, tested and evaluated, and any issues need to be fixed and tested again before deployment.

Ayush built an automation agent around that complete lifecycle. It starts from an agent’s purpose and required tools, builds the workflow, runs evaluations and repeats the fix-and-validation loop until the agent is ready to deploy.

A later inbound-campaign update described the same direction of continuous improvement: analyse previous call transcriptions, identify issues and improve future calls. It also distinguished the measured campaign results from rollout experiments and future plans.
solutions: Build the workflow from its purpose
The automation takes the intended purpose and tools of an ElevenLabs agent and creates the workflow around them. It brings workflow creation and test/evaluation setup into the same process.
Close the test-and-fix loop
The agent runs evaluations, identifies issues, makes fixes and reruns the evaluations. The July update described this as a complete build–test–fix–validate loop supporting deployment readiness.
Deploy the follow-up campaigns

The update reported the BC2V Missed Visit Long Follow-up agent and the workflow-based A2I Missed Inspection campaign deployed to production. A separate BI2BC Customer Finance flow was described as production-ready, rather than already deployed.
Use conversations to improve future calls

The later inbound-campaign update described transcription analysis feeding issue identification and agent improvements. Customer context from Chronicle was also integrated, with the contextualised agent launched at 10% of volume across India.
outcomes: Two campaigns deployed through the workflow
The 12 July update reported two follow-up campaigns in production after the build-and-validation loop. The separate Customer Finance flow had reached production readiness.
Campaign results reported with their measurement period

The 27 July update reported AI V2 visit conversion of 5.24% and delivery conversion of 0.66%, against human-calling figures of 5.12% and 0.62%. The data covered 27 April–20 July, and the latest delivery results were still maturing.
productAlt: Published AI V2 inbound campaign results shared in the July release update
statsAsOf: 27 July 2026 update: conversion data covers 27 April–20 July; contextual-agent rollout reported separately.

name: Mayank
description: Created Design Audit, a reusable skill that checks design-system usage, content and accessibility, then adds Dev Mode findings and proposes fixes for review.
title: Making design review a reusable skill.
challenge: A design review needs to establish whether a screen uses approved components and tokens, while also checking copy, calculations, image–text consistency and basic usability. A component that looks correct can still be detached from its source library.

Mayank created Design Audit as a reusable skill across Codex, Claude Code and Figma Agent. It checks actual library usage, finds inconsistencies and makes findings visible through Dev Mode annotations and a report.

The first version was shared for small-screen trials. Its proposed fixes are reviewed before being applied, and its results depend on the agent’s Figma access and ability to inspect the required libraries.
solutions: Check the approved design-system sources

The skill checks widgets, components, atoms, icons, tokens and typography against five approved libraries. It distinguishes actual source identifiers from a visual or naming match and looks for detached instances and hard-coded values.
Review content and interface consistency

The checks cover placeholders, inconsistent copy, calculations and image–text mismatches. They also consider contrast, touch-target sizes, spacing and component variants, making the review broader than a token-only check.
Put findings where designers review them

Findings appear as Dev Mode annotations with a summary report. The reusable skill file works across the three supported agents, provided the Figma connection has the required access and script-execution support.
Keep fixes reviewable
The skill can propose supported token fixes and apply them after approval. The initial release invited trials on a small screen and feedback on missed issues, false positives and setup problems.
outcomeTitle: An initial version ready for trials.
outcomes: An initial version shared for trials
Mayank shared Design Audit on 19 October 2026, with a team guide covering installation, commands and capabilities. It was an initial release, rather than a claim of broad adoption.
A repeatable review workflow
The contribution combines source-library checks, content review and Dev Mode findings in one reusable skill. Supported fixes remain subject to approval rather than being applied without review.

name: Ishaan Kothiyal
description: Shared reusable design-system skills and a Design Audit guide to help teams build and review AI-assisted interfaces.
title: Making the design system usable by AI.
challengeTitle: AI output needs a shared design foundation.
challenge: An AI-generated interface can look plausible without using the approved components, typography or tokens. Teams need reusable instructions and a reliable way to check what an agent produces.
Ishaan shared a collection of ten design-system skill packages and a team guide for Design Audit. The materials give designers and engineers a common starting point for AI-assisted UI work.
solutions: Share reusable design-system skills

The collection covers platform UI, components, design tokens, desktop and mobile typography, icons, primitive and semantic colors, borders and radius. Ishaan shared the ten packages with the design team in March 2026.
Make review repeatable

His Design Audit team guide explains how to check Figma designs against approved source libraries, inspect tokens and UI consistency, and review findings through Dev Mode annotations and a report. It also explains when checks must remain unverified.
Test the workflow with a team
In October, Ishaan shared the team’s Codex and Figma experiment for generating a V3 homepage draft directly in the CMS, including page creation, asset uploads, token mapping and visual QA.
Be clear about the remaining work

The demo was an early prototype. Ishaan identified gaps in pixel accuracy, carousel and asset extraction, unsupported effects and component coverage. Manual review and developer input were still needed.
outcomeTitle: Reusable foundations, with the limits made visible.
outcomes: A shared starting point
The uploaded skill packages and audit guide make design-system guidance available for repeated AI-assisted building and review, rather than relying only on one-off prompts.
A tested direction for the team

The CMS proof of concept produced a usable homepage draft. Ishaan credited the team behind the experiment and described broader page coverage and team training as next steps, not completed production automation.
productAlt: Ten design-system skill packages shared by Ishaan Kothiyal in March 2026
